            return null;

        if (type === 'CustomEvent' && msg.includes('unhandledrejection')) {

</script>                                <p class="wp-block-paragraph">To deploy a Node.js application, you can either follow a general deployment workflow that works across most hosting environments or use hosting-specific options like web app hosting or a virtual private server (VPS).</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Node.js deployment means moving your application from a local development machine to a production server where users can access it over the internet.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Proper deployment directly affects how your Node.js application performs under real traffic. A misconfigured server can cause slow response times, unexpected downtime, or security vulnerabilities that expose sensitive data.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Setting up the Node.js production environment correctly from the start helps prevent these issues and keeps the application stable as traffic grows.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">The typical Node.js deployment process includes five stages: preparation, hosting selection, environment configuration, deployment, and monitoring.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Here’s what each stage involves:</p><ol class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Prepare the production application.</strong> Define dependencies in <strong>package.json</strong>, configure environment variables, and add a start script.</li>



<li><strong>Commit and push the code to Git.</strong> Upload files to the repository using the browser interface or run Git CLI commands from your computer.</li>



<li><strong>Set up Node.js and a process manager.</strong> Install Node.js on the server, configure environment variables, and use PM2 to keep the application running after crashes or reboots.</li>



<li><strong>Route traffic through a reverse proxy.</strong> Configure NGINX to forward requests to the Node.js process on its internal port and secure connections with an SSL certificate.</li>



<li><strong>Verify and monitor the deployment.</strong> Check the application in the browser, review PM2 logs, and monitor performance metrics to detect issues early.</li>
</ol><p class="wp-block-paragraph"></p><h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-how-to-deploy-a-node-js-application"><strong>How to deploy a Node.js application</strong></h2><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Deploying a <a href="/tutorials/what-is-node-js/" data-wpel-link="internal" rel="follow">Node.js</a> application follows a universal workflow that works regardless of the hosting provider.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">The core process includes preparing the app for production, pushing the code to Git, setting up the server with a process manager, configuring a reverse proxy with HTTPS, and testing the live deployment.</p><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>1. </strong><strong>Prepare the Node.js application for deployment</strong></h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Preparing a Node.js application for deployment means making sure the project includes everything a production server needs to install dependencies and start the app automatically.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Three files form the foundation of a deployment-ready Node.js project: <strong>app.js</strong> (the main application file), <strong>package.json</strong> (project metadata, dependencies, and scripts), and <strong>.gitignore</strong> (files excluded from version control).</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Every package your application imports must appear under the <strong>dependencies</strong> field in <strong>package.json</strong>. The file tells <strong>npm</strong> install which packages to download on the server.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">If a required package is missing, the application will crash in production even if it worked locally, where the package already existed in <strong>node_modules</strong>. Here’s an example:</p><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">{
   "name": "node-deploy-test",
   "version": "1.0.0",
   "description": "Sample Node.js app for deployment tutorial",
   "main": "app.js",
   "scripts": {
      "start": "node app.js"
   },
   "dependencies": {
      "express": "^4.21.0"
   }
}</pre><p class="wp-block-paragraph">The scripts section defines how <a href="/tutorials/best-node-js-hosting/" data-wpel-link="internal" rel="follow">Node.js hosting platforms</a> and process managers start the application. The <strong>“start”: “node app.js”</strong> entry tells the server to run <strong>app.js</strong> as the entry point.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Node.js environment variables store configuration values that change between environments, such as development and production. Use them for values such as port numbers, database credentials, and API keys, rather than hardcoding them in source files.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">In the application code, reference these values using <strong>process.env</strong>:</p><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;</pre><p class="wp-block-paragraph">This line reads the <strong>PORT</strong> variable if it exists. Otherwise, it defaults to <strong>3000</strong>. The same pattern applies to <strong>NODE_ENV</strong>, which hosting platforms usually set to production automatically.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Keeping configuration in environment variables prevents sensitive data from leaking into your repository. It also lets you change settings for each environment without modifying the code.</p><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>2. Push the application code to a Git repository</strong></h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Version control is essential for Node.js deployment because it creates a reliable, trackable record of every change to the codebase.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">If a deployment introduces a bug, you can revert to the last working commit in seconds, rather than blindly troubleshooting.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Git is the standard version control system, and GitHub is the most common platform for hosting Git repositories. Start by creating a repository on GitHub:</p><ol class="wp-block-list">
<li>Log in to GitHub, or create an account at <strong>github.com</strong> if you don’t have one.</li>



<li>Click <strong>New</strong> on the dashboard, then enter a repository name, for example, <strong>node-deploy-test</strong>.</li>



<li>Set the visibility to <strong>Public</strong> if you plan to connect the repository to a hosting platform later.</li>



<li>Leave the other options unchecked (no <strong>README</strong>, no <strong>.gitignore</strong>, no license), then click <strong>Create repository</strong>.</li>

<li>On the repository setup page, click <strong>uploading an existing file</strong>.</li>



<li>Drag <strong>app.js</strong> and <strong>package.json</strong> into the upload area.</li>



<li>Click <strong>Commit changes</strong>.</li>
</ol><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Keep in mind that most operating systems hide dotfiles like <strong>.gitignore</strong>, so drag-and-drop uploads won’t work. Create the file directly on GitHub instead:</p><ol class="wp-block-list">
<li>On the repository’s main page, click <strong>Add file</strong> → <strong>Create new file</strong>.</li>



<li>Type <strong>.gitignore</strong> as the filename and add the following line as its content:</li>
</ol><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">node_modules/</pre><ol start="3" class="wp-block-list">
<li>Click <strong>Commit changes</strong>.</li>
</ol><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Alternatively, if Git is installed on your computer, you can push all your files, including <strong>.gitignore</strong>, using <a href="/tutorials/basic-git-commands/" data-wpel-link="internal" rel="follow">Git CLI commands</a>:</p><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">cd path/to/node-deploy-test
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/node-deploy-test.git
git push -u origin main</pre><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Replace <strong>your-username</strong> with your actual GitHub username.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">The Git CLI method works better for ongoing development. Running <strong>git push</strong> sends only the changes, while browser uploads require you to upload files again.</p><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>3. Set up the server and run the application</strong></h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Setting up the server starts with installing Node.js. You can install it using Node Version Manager (NVM) or a system package manager.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">NVM is the better option because it lets you install and switch between multiple Node.js versions without requiring root permissions.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Node.js processes stop when the terminal session closes or when the server reboots. This means a crash can take the application offline until someone manually restarts it.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">PM2, a production-grade Node.js process manager, solves this problem. It runs the application as a background daemon and automatically restarts it after failures or server reboots.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">At this point, the application runs internally on a port such as <strong>3000</strong>, but users still can’t access it through standard web ports like <strong>80</strong> or <strong>443</strong>. To expose the application to the public internet, you need to set up a reverse proxy.</p><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>4. Configure a reverse proxy and enable HTTPS</strong></h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">A reverse proxy server like NGINX routes public traffic to the Node.js application running on an internal port.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">NGINX listens on ports <strong>80</strong> (HTTP) and <strong>443</strong> (HTTPS), accepts incoming requests, and forwards them to <strong>localhost:3000</strong> or to whichever port your app uses. Users never interact with the Node.js process directly.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">This setup also serves as the termination point for SSL/TLS connections, keeping encryption management separate from your application code.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">After configuring the reverse proxy, enable HTTPS using Certbot with a Let’s Encrypt SSL certificate.</p><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>5. Test and monitor the deployed application</strong></h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">After deployment, test the Node.js application by opening a browser and visiting your application’s root URL, for example, <strong>http://domain.tld</strong>. The main page should load with the expected content.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">If you added a health check route, append <strong>/health</strong> to your application’s URL and confirm it returns JSON output like:</p><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">{"status":"healthy","uptime":...}</pre><div class="wp-block-image">

For PM2, the<strong> pm2 logs</strong> command shows a real-time stream of your application’s output and error messages.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">For a broader view, run <strong>pm2 monit</strong> to open an interactive dashboard. It shows CPU usage, memory consumption, event loop latency, and logs in one place.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">As a baseline, a healthy Node.js application typically stays under 50 ms event loop latency, uses around 300–500 MB of memory for a standard Express app, and keeps CPU usage below 70% under normal traffic.</p><h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-how-to-deploy-a-node-js-application-using-web-app-hosting"><strong>How to deploy a Node.js application using web app hosting</strong></h2><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Deploying a Node.js application with web app hosting involves connecting a Git repository, defining build commands, and triggering deployment from a dashboard.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Hostinger Node.js web app hosting provides a managed hosting environment that lets you deploy applications without setting up a server from scratch.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">It handles the underlying infrastructure, including server configuration, Node.js installation, process management, and SSL certificates.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">It also supports automatic redeployment, so when you push changes to GitHub, the system rebuilds and redeploys your application automatically.</p><p>

</div><p class="wp-block-paragraph">You can adjust these settings if your project needs different values:</p><ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Framework preset.</strong> The detected framework for your project, for example, Express.js. Change it if auto-detection selects the wrong one.</li>



<li><strong>Node.js version.</strong> The runtime version for your application. The system detects this from the engines field in <strong>package.json</strong>, but you can override it manually.</li>



<li><strong>Entry file.</strong> The file the server runs to start the application. It defaults to <strong>app.js</strong>, based on the Node.js start command in <strong>package.json</strong>.</li>



<li><strong>Package manager.</strong> The tool used to install dependencies. By default, it’s <strong>npm</strong>, but you can switch to <strong>Yarn</strong> or <strong>pnpm</strong> if your project uses a different lock file.</li>



<li><strong>Environment variables.</strong> Production values like API keys or database credentials. Add them here instead of committing them to the repository.</li>
</ul><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>4. Launch and verify the deployed application</strong></h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Click <strong>Deploy</strong> to start the build. <li><strong>GitHub repository link.</strong> Opens the connected repository in a new tab so you can review code, branches, or recent commits.</li>



<li><strong>Last deployment details.</strong> Shows the deployment status (<strong>success</strong> or <strong>failure</strong>), the timestamp, and a link to the full deployment log.</li>



<li><strong>Quick links.</strong> Jump directly to <strong>Deployments</strong>, <strong>Environment Variables</strong>, <strong>Settings & Redeploy</strong>, or <strong>File Manager</strong>.</li>



<li><strong>Resource usage graphs.</strong> Show average CPU, RAM, and I/O usage. If any metric approaches the red dotted line, which marks your plan’s limit, consider upgrading.</li>
</ul><h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-how-to-deploy-a-node-js-application-using-vps-hosting"><strong>How to deploy a Node.js application using VPS hosting</strong></h2><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Deploying a Node.js application on a VPS involves connecting to a remote server via SSH, installing Node.js, uploading your application code, setting up a process manager and reverse proxy, and enabling HTTPS.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph"><a href="/vps-hosting" data-wpel-link="internal" rel="follow">VPS hosting</a> gives you full control over the server environment so that you can configure everything from the operating system to firewall rules.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">This approach requires more setup than managed web app hosting. export PORT=3000</pre><p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>NODE_ENV=production</strong> tells frameworks to optimize for performance and disable development features. <strong>PORT</strong> should match the port your application listens on, as configured in <strong>app.js</strong>.</p><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>4. Configure PM2 and reverse proxy</strong></h3><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Start your Node.js application with PM2 to keep it running in the background.</p><ol class="wp-block-list">
<li>Install PM2 and start the application:</li>
</ol><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">npm install -g pm2
pm2 start app.js --name "node-app"</pre><ol start="2" class="wp-block-list">
<li>Configure PM2 to restart the application after a server reboot:</li>
</ol><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">pm2 startup
pm2 save</pre><p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>pm2 startup</strong> generates a system service that launches PM2 on boot. <strong>pm2 save</strong> persists the current process list so PM2 knows which applications to restart.</p><ol start="3" class="wp-block-list">
<li>Open firewall ports for web traffic. Otherwise, NGINX won’t receive incoming connections:</li>

</ol><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">apt update
apt install nginx -y</pre><ol start="5" class="wp-block-list">
<li><a href="/tutorials/how-to-set-up-nginx-reverse-proxy/" data-wpel-link="internal" rel="follow">Create an NGINX reverse proxy</a> configuration for your Node.js deployment:</li>
</ol><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/node-app</pre><ol start="6" class="wp-block-list">
<li>Add the following configuration, replacing <strong>your-hostname</strong> with your own domain name or server hostname:</li>
</ol><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">server {
   listen 80;
   server_name your-hostname;

   location / {
      proxy_pass http://localhost:3000;
      proxy_http_version 1.1;
      proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
      proxy_set_header Connection 'upgrade';
      proxy_set_header Host $host;
      proxy_cache_bypass $http_upgrade;
   }
}</pre><div class="wp-block-image">

<li>Enable HTTPS with Certbot. Make sure your domain or hostname points to the server’s IP address, since Certbot can’t issue certificates for IP addresses.</li>
</ol><pre class="EnlighterJSRAW" data-enlighter-language="generic" data-enlighter-theme="" data-enlighter-highlight="" data-enlighter-linenumbers="" data-enlighter-lineoffset="" data-enlighter-title="" data-enlighter-group="">apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx -y
certbot --nginx -d your-hostname</pre><ol start="12" class="wp-block-list">
<li>Follow the prompts to enter an email address and accept the terms. Certbot verifies domain ownership, issues the certificate, and automatically updates the NGINX configuration to redirect HTTP traffic to HTTPS.</li>
</ol><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Once done, visit your application’s URL again and confirm that the “Connection is secure” message appears in your browser.</p><h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>5. </div><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Press <strong>Ctrl + C</strong> to exit any of these views.</p><h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-what-are-the-best-practices-for-node-js-deployment"><strong>What are the best practices for Node.js deployment?</strong></h2><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Best practices for Node.js deployment focus on automation, environment separation, and proactive monitoring to keep production applications stable and secure.</p><ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Set up a </strong><strong>CI/CD</strong><strong> pipeline.</strong> Use tools like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, or Jenkins to run your test suite on every commit and automatically deploy when all tests pass. This removes manual deployment steps and helps catch bugs before they reach production.</li>



<li><strong>Separate configuration from code.</strong> Store environment-specific values in environment variables or external config files that you don’t commit to the repository. Use a <strong>.env</strong> file locally, loaded with a library like <strong>dotenv</strong>, and set variables directly on the server or through your hosting platform’s dashboard in production.</li>



<li><strong>Use structured logging.</strong> Log in JSON format so tools like the ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or Datadog can parse and search logs efficiently. Include a timestamp, log level, and request ID in each entry to trace issues across requests.</li>



<li><strong>Set up automated health checks.</strong> Use a monitoring service like UptimeRobot or Pingdom to ping your application’s health endpoint every 30–60 seconds. If the endpoint fails or returns an error, the service sends alerts through email, Slack, or SMS so you can respond before users notice. As a baseline, aim to keep p95 response time under 200 ms.</li>



<li><strong>Enable automated rollbacks.</strong> Configure your CI/CD pipeline to redeploy the last stable version if a new release fails health checks or crashes within a set window, for example, three restarts within five minutes. PM2 supports this with the <strong>–max-restarts</strong> flag, and tools like GitHub Actions can trigger a rollback when the deployment script fails.</li>
</ul><h2 class="wp-block-heading" id="h-how-to-scale-a-node-js-application-in-production"><strong>How to scale a Node.js application in production</strong></h2><p class="wp-block-paragraph">To scale a Node.js application in production, combine server-level strategies with architectural changes that distribute traffic and workload across multiple processes or machines.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Horizontal scaling</strong> adds more server instances to handle increased traffic, with a load balancer distributing requests between them.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Vertical scaling</strong> increases resources like CPU, RAM, and storage on a single server. It’s simpler to set up, but it has limits because a single machine can only scale so far.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Load balancing</strong> distributes requests evenly, preventing any single process from becoming a bottleneck. NGINX can act as a load balancer by defining an upstream block with multiple backend servers and routing traffic between them.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Node.js runs on a single thread by default, so it uses only one CPU core even if the server has more available.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">The built-in <strong>cluster</strong> module solves this by forking the main process into multiple worker processes, usually one per CPU core, all sharing the same server port.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">PM2 simplifies clustering with cluster mode. Running <strong>pm2 start app.js -i max</strong> spawns one worker per available CPU core automatically.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">For larger setups, containerization with Docker packages your Node.js application and its dependencies into a portable image that runs consistently across environments.</p><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Tools like <a href="/tutorials/kubernetes-tutorial/" data-wpel-link="internal" rel="follow">Kubernetes</a> manage containers across multiple machines. They handle scaling, rolling updates, health checks, and load balancing automatically.</p>

                const isHostingerUserLoggedIn = function () {

                            return cookie

                                .startsWith( configuration.cookieName + '=' );
                        } );

                 *
                 * @param {string} clickElement Click element identifier.
                 *
                 * @return {void}
                 */
                const sendGsiAmplitudeEvent = function ( clickElement ) {
                    if (
                        'function' !== typeof window.hgrSendAmplitudeEvent
                    ) {
                        return;
                    }

                    window.hgrSendAmplitudeEvent(
                        {
                            name: configuration.amplitudeEventName,
                            properties: {
                                clickElement: clickElement,
                            },
                        }
                    );
                };

                /**
                 * Handle a Google Identity Services prompt moment notification.
                 *
                 * @param {PromptMomentNotification} moment Prompt notification.
                 *
                 * @return {void}
                 */
                window.logMomentNotification = function ( moment ) {
                    if (
                        ! moment
                        || 'function' !== typeof moment.getMomentType
                    ) {
                        return;
                    }

                    const momentType = moment.getMomentType();
                    let reason;

                    if (
                        'function' === typeof moment.isDismissedMoment
                        && moment.isDismissedMoment()
                        && 'function' === typeof moment.getDismissedReason
                    ) {
                        reason = moment.getDismissedReason();
                    }

                    let clickElement =
                        configuration.amplitudeClickElementPrefix
                        + '-'
                        + momentType;

                    if ( reason ) {
                        clickElement += '-' + reason;
                    }

                    sendGsiAmplitudeEvent( clickElement );
                };

                /**
                 * Create the Google Identity Services configuration element.
                 *
                 * @return {void}
                 */
                const createGsiContainer = function () {
                    if ( document.getElementById( 'g_id_onload' ) ) {
                        return;
                    }

                    const container = document.createElement( 'div' );

                    container.id = 'g_id_onload';
                    container.dataset.client_id = configuration.clientId;
                    container.dataset.login_uri = configuration.loginUri;
                    container.dataset.ux_mode = 'redirect';
                    container.dataset.cancel_on_tap_outside = 'false';
                    container.dataset.context = 'signin';
                    container.dataset.auto_prompt = 'true';
                    container.dataset.itp_support = 'true';
                    container.dataset.state = configuration.state;
